She woke on the first morning of the year to find that something was terribly wrong. Her fishtail—the sleek, shimmering length of her that had carried her through every current of her life—had simply vanished. In its place, tangled somewhere in the sheets beside her, were two strange and unfamiliar appendages, cold to the touch and utterly foreign.

At first, she was certain it was a joke. The staff had been drinking heavily the night before, ringing in the New Year with far too much enthusiasm, and this seemed exactly the sort of prank they might play. Disgusted, she seized the peculiar limbs and flung them out of the room, expecting to be rid of them for good.

What followed left her thoroughly bewildered. As the limbs went sailing away, she found herself tumbling helplessly out of bed after them, crashing to the floor in a heap. It made no sense to her at all. She could not yet comprehend the simple, astonishing truth: those cold appendages were not a prank left by careless hands—they were attached to her own body.

It fell to her sister to explain what had happened. Gently, patiently, she told her that she now had two legs where her tail had once been, and that she would have to learn how to use them—how to stand, how to balance, how to walk across solid ground as the land-dwellers did.

In the months that followed, the narrator often found herself dwelling on that strange transformation. She wondered, with a quiet melancholy, whether her spirits had somehow fallen along with the arches of her new feet—whether the sinking she felt inside was tied, in some inexplicable way, to the collapse of those tender insteps beneath her.

# The Thingammies

The first thing Coralie noticed was the strangeness of the morning light filtering through the water above her chamber. The second thing she noticed was that something was terribly wrong with her tail.

She reached down beneath the woven kelp blanket, expecting the familiar smooth scales, the powerful sweep of fin that had carried her through the currents since the day she was born. Instead, her fingers met something else entirely—two long, pale things splitting off from her body where her tail should have been. Two separate things, ending in strange flat appendages with tiny nubs at their tips.

"Very funny," she muttered, still half-asleep. Someone had played a trick on her. Her cousins, most likely, or those wretched twins from the eastern reef. They were always up to mischief. They must have attached these ridiculous *thingammies* to her while she slept, these floppy, useless imitations of a proper tail.

With a irritated flick of her wrists, she flung them away from her, expecting them to detach and drift off into the water. They did not. Instead, her whole lower body lurched, and to her horror the *thingammies* moved *with* her, dragging the rest of her along with them. She tumbled sideways, tangled in her blanket, and fell right out of her bed onto the sandy floor of her chamber.

She lay there, stunned, staring at the two things now sprawled awkwardly before her. They ended in what looked like small paddles, each divided into five wriggling parts. When she tried to move them, they obeyed—clumsily, tentatively—but they obeyed. They were *hers*.

The truth crept over her slowly, cold as a deep-sea current.

"Sister?" Marisol appeared in the doorway, her own silver tail catching the light, and stopped when she saw Coralie on the floor, trembling. Her expression was not one of surprise, but of gentle, aching sorrow. She had known this was coming.

"They're called *legs*," Marisol said softly, kneeling beside her. "The sea witch kept her word. This is what you asked for, Coralie. This is what you wanted."

Coralie could not speak. She looked at the legs—her legs—and tried to remember the wish that had brought her here, the desperate longing that had seemed so clear beneath the moonlit surface. It had felt like the only thing in the world worth having. Now, sprawled on the floor of the only home she had ever known, unable to swim, unable even to stand, she felt only a vast and dizzying loss.

Marisol helped her back onto the bed, arranged the useless legs as best she could, and stayed with her while the confusion settled into something heavier and more permanent.

The months that followed were the hardest Coralie had ever known. She had to learn everything anew—how to balance, how to bear her own weight, how to move these foreign limbs that ached and buckled and refused to understand her. There were nights she wept for her lost tail, for the effortless grace of the water, for the person she had been before she traded it all away. There were mornings she woke and forgot, and reached down, and grieved all over again.

She had wanted this. She had to keep reminding herself of that. But no one had told her that getting exactly what you wish for can break your heart just as surely as never getting it at all. No one had told her that transformation, however complete, still leaves you carrying the ghost of everything you used to be.

Slowly—so slowly—she learned to stand. And though she never quite stopped missing the sea, she began, at last, to walk.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short story about a mermaid who wakes up one morning to discover she has human legs, using irreverent, colloquial British slang and a darkly comic tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# Legs Eleven

Coralie woke up with what can only be described as the world's worst hangover and two absolutely ludicrous appendages where her tail used to be.

"Oh, you're having a laugh," she said to no one, because no one lived at the bottom of the sea except her and a judgmental crab named Kevin.

She stared at the things. Legs. Great pale wobbling legs, all knees and hair and stupid little toes wiggling about like startled sea slugs. Where her glorious iridescent tail had been—the one that took her three hundred years to grow, thank you very much—there was now this. This *situation*.

"Right," she said, "someone's taking the piss."

Kevin scuttled over, waved a claw in a manner that could only be interpreted as *cor, that's rough, that is*, and buggered off to hide under a rock. Bloody typical. Fair-weather crab, that one.

The problem, Coralie quickly discovered, was that legs don't work underwater. They just sort of... dangle. Useless flappy meat-sticks. She'd been the fastest swimmer in the entire western trench, and now she was doggy-paddling about like a drowned Labrador, cursing every deity she could think of, which as a pagan sea-creature was quite a lot.

"Ursula, you absolute cow," she muttered, on the off chance this was some witch's doing. Though frankly it was probably her own fault. She *had* made a wish on a falling star last night, hadn't she? After too much fermented kelp? Something soppy about wanting to know what it felt like to *walk on the beach with someone*. God, how embarrassing. Drunk-wishing. The magical equivalent of texting your ex.

Getting to the surface was a nightmare. She kicked and floundered and swallowed roughly nine gallons of the Atlantic before hauling herself, gasping and furious, onto a pebbly beach somewhere near what a nearby sign informed her was *Skegness*.

"Skegness," she wheezed, flat on her back. "I sacrificed my tail for *Skegness*."

The legs, now that she was on land, seemed keen to actually do something. She stood up. Immediately fell over. Stood up again, wobbled like a newborn foal that had been at the gin, and managed three whole steps before face-planting into a discarded chip wrapper.

"Alright, love?" said a man walking a small aggressive dog. "You look proper worse for wear."

"I've lost my tail," Coralie said with tremendous dignity, mayonnaise on her chin.

"Haven't we all, darling," he said, and carried on walking.

She sat there for a while, contemplating. The sun was doing something quite nice on the water. Somewhere a seagull was murdering a pasty. And Coralie, three-hundred-and-seventy years old and newly bipedal, felt the strangest thing bubbling up inside her.

Not sadness. Not exactly.

Curiosity.

Because down in the trench there was nothing but darkness and cold and Kevin's disapproval and the endless bloody quiet. And up here—well. Up here there were chips. And that man's terrible little dog. And a whole gormless world of nonsense she'd never seen.

She heaved herself upright one more time, arms windmilling, and took a step. Then another. Then a third, giggling now, this mad half-drowned creature learning to walk on a freezing beach in the arse-end of Lincolnshire.

"Right then," she said to the wobbling legs. "Go on. Impress me."

They didn't, particularly. She fell over twice more and cried a bit and definitely got sand in places sand should never go.

But she walked.

And somewhere out in the grey water, Kevin the crab watched her stagger off toward the amusement arcade, waved one claw in something that might have been farewell, and thought, in the only language crabs know:

*Silly cow'll be back by Tuesday.*

He wasn't wrong. But that's another story entirely.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell the Little Mermaid transformation from the mermaid's confused first-person perspective, as if she doesn't understand what legs are and thinks the hospital staff are pranking her on New Year's Eve.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Trade

I don't understand what's happening.

The Sea Witch promised me *feet*—she said it like I should know what they are. I said yes because I love him, and now everything is white and too bright and smells like nothing, like the ocean drained itself while I slept.

There are people around me in matching coverings. They keep saying words. "Recovery." "The anesthesia." "Can you wiggle your toes for me, sweetheart?"

**Toes.** Another word from the sorceress's spell, apparently. What is a toe. I try to swish my tail and—

It doesn't swish.

It *splits.*

I scream, except I can't, because that was the price, wasn't it? My voice. So I open my mouth and nothing comes out and one of them pats my hand and says "Happy New Year, hon, you came through great."

*New Year.* Is this the ritual? Is this what land-people do—cut a girl in half at the turning of the year and call it *great?* They keep looking at a device that beeps. I think they're timing something. A countdown.

I look down. Where my beautiful tail was, there are two pale things. They *bend.* In the middle. Independently. It's the most horrifying thing I've ever witnessed. One of the coverings-people sees my face and laughs—*laughs*—and says, "First time's always a shock. You'll be dancing by summer."

Dancing. Another agony-word. The witch mentioned dancing. She said every step would feel like knives.

They are *definitely* pranking me.

They keep sliding these fabric-tubes over the split-things. "Compression socks," they say, like it's normal to sheathe a person's new nightmare-limbs in cloth. Somewhere a horn blows. Voices count backward. *Ten. Nine.*

I don't have a voice to ask what I've become.

*Eight. Seven.*

The prince isn't even here.

*Six.*

I wiggle a toe.

The whole room cheers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental flash fiction about a sea creature adjusting to a human body, blending humor and melancholy, and ending on a bittersweet note about her heart and her fallen arches.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Matter of Feet

The pamphlet had said nothing about feet.

It had said much about *love*—that human word, all consonants and commitment—and something about *legs*, which the sea witch delivered as promised, twin and pale and prone to bruising. But feet were an afterthought of the transformation, a footnote, and now they ache.

I had gills once. Do you understand what I am telling you? I breathed the whole ocean. I did not *sip* at air like this, apologetic, through a nose that runs when I weep, which is often, because human eyes are always leaking something. Below, we wept and no one noticed. Here, my grief has weather. It has a face.

The prince is kind. This is the cruelty of it. If he were wicked I could go home—swim back down the pamphlet's fine print and demand a refund of my voice. But he is kind, and he brings me *shoes*, which are little coffins for the parts of me that used to be a tail. He does not know I once outraced sharks. He thinks I am delicate because I fall down. I fall down because the ground refuses to move and I have not forgiven it.

Things I did not anticipate, in no order, for order is a land-invention:

That stairs would be a philosophy.

That I would miss *salt* the way one misses a mother.

That laughter, up here, requires the same muscles as drowning, and I would confuse the two at dinner parties.

That I would love him anyway. Stupidly. Fully. With a heart that thumps *in air*, exposed, unbuoyed, doing all its labor without the water's help.

Let me tell you about the heart. Below, it floated. Here it hangs in me like a bell with no rope, ringing at the sight of him, ringing when he sleeps, ringing at the gulls who know my sisters and will not carry a message.

And let me tell you, last, about my arches.

They have fallen.

The doctor—a human word for *someone who names your ruin*—pressed his thumb along my sole and said, *fallen arches*, as though my feet had once stood tall and proud and had simply given up, the way I have given up the tide, the way I have given up the language of currents, the way I am, slowly, giving up the girl who could hold her breath forever because she had no breath to hold.

So here I am. A creature of impossible depths, undone by gravity.

My heart, that traitor, still floats toward him.

My arches, those honest things, have finally told the truth: that some of us were never built to stand on land, only to *long* from it—

and oh, how beautifully, how permanently,

I long.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a whimsical, offbeat story in a distinctly British working-class voice about someone waking up with mysterious "thingammies" attached to her that turn out to be legs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Them Thingammies

Right, so I wakes up Tuesday morning—least I *think* it were Tuesday, could've been Wednesday, all them days blur into one great gray porridge once you've hit sixty-odd—and there's these two *things* dangling off the bottom of me.

Long, they was. Pinkish. With little knobbly bits at the ends like someone'd stuck a bunch of chipolatas together and thought better of it halfway through.

"Ere," I says, out loud, to nobody, on account of Derek's been dead these fourteen years and the cat buggered off in March. "What in the name of all that's holy are them thingammies?"

Now I'm not one to panic. Me mam always said, "Sheila, you could sleep through the Blitz and complain about the noise the next mornin'," and she weren't wrong. So I gives one of these thingummybobs a bit of a prod, and—stone me—it *moves*. Sort of twitches. Like a landed haddock having second thoughts.

"Well I never," I says.

I has a proper think about it over me first fag of the day. Puzzler, this. I tries to remember if I'd ordered owt off the telly. You know how it is at three in the mornin' when you can't sleep and there's a fella on the shopping channel selling contraptions—them foldy-uppy exercise machines, them non-stick fry pans what stick regardless. Maybe, thinks I, I'd gone and ordered a set of them thingammies in a moment of weakness. Two for the price of one, no doubt. There's always two for the price of one.

But no. No receipt on the mantelpiece. No box.

So I gets Denise on the blower. Denise knows things. Denise did a course once.

"Denise," I says. "I've woke up with a pair of thingammies attached to me and I can't for the life of me work out what they're for."

Long pause, there were. Then Denise says, all careful like, "Sheila, love... describe 'em to me."

So I does. Long. Pinkish. Chipolata ends. Bit of hair on 'em what I'm not proud of.

And Denise, she goes very quiet, and then she says the daftest thing I ever did hear.

"Sheila," she says. "Them's your *legs*."

Well.

I sat there. And I looked at 'em. And I thought—*legs*. Course. LEGS. I've had 'em all along, haven't I! It's just I've not had proper cause to think about 'em in donkey's years, what with the mobility scooter and the stairlift and the good Lord's provision of a downstairs commode. Forgot I owned the buggers, didn't I. Filed 'em under "miscellaneous" like everyone does with knees and elbows and that flap of skin under your chin what waves goodbye after you've stopped.

"Legs," I says to Denise. "Well what am I meant to do with *them* at my time of life?"

And Denise, bless her, she says, "You could try *standin'* on 'em, Sheila."

Standin'. On 'em. What a notion.

So I has another fag to steel meself, and I swings the pair of 'em round off the bed, and I plants them chipolata ends on the lino—cold, that lino, freezes yer to the bone—and I gives it a heave.

And UP I comes.

Wobblin' like a jelly at a christening, mind. Hands out like I'm walkin' a tightrope over the Grand Canyon. But UP. Vertical. Tall as a house, felt like, though I'm four foot eleven in me slippers and always have been.

"DENISE!" I hollers into the phone what's still on the bed a mile below me. "DENISE, I'M UPRIGHT!"

And I takes a step. And then another. Great wobbling lurchy things, like a foal what's been at the sherry, but *steps*, and I gets meself all the way to the window, and I pulls back the nets, and I looks out at Coronation Street—the *actual* street, not the telly one—and there's little Kevin from number six kicking a ball, and there's the bins wants doin', and there's the whole grey glorious lot of it.

And I stood there. On me thingammies. On me *legs*.

"You still there, Denise?" I says, once I'd shuffled back and picked up the phone.

"I'm here, love."

"I might," I says, and I'm all choked up now, silly cow that I am, "I might just walk to the shop. On these. Get meself a scratch card and a nice bit of ham."

And Denise says, "You do that, Sheila."

So I did.

Took me an hour and a half and I had to sit on three separate walls and a bus shelter, but I did.

Bloody marvellous, legs. Should've had a go on 'em years ago.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a modern, gritty, funny reimagining of a mermaid losing her tail, told with disorientation and unusual metaphors like kelp and ham, transitioning into a wistful reflection on learning to walk.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Molting

The tail went first, which is a stupid way to say it because the tail was *me*—the tail was seventy percent of my available real estate and one hundred percent of my personality—but there I was on the tideline like a dropped sandwich, watching the thing that used to be my everything peel off in strips.

It didn't hurt. That's the part nobody warns you about. It felt like taking off a wetsuit that had opinions. It felt like the moment a name leaves your mouth and you realize you've been saying it wrong your whole life. The scales came away wet and glittering and useless, kelp-slick, and underneath were these two obscene pink things I would later learn to call *legs*, though at the time I filed them under *ham*. Two hams. Cold, twitching, salt-crusted hams where my exquisite emerald self had been.

I remember thinking: *this is the worst haircut in maritime history.*

The world up here is loud in a way that has nothing to do with volume. Underwater, sound arrives like weather—it surrounds you, it's ambient, it's a mood. Up here sound comes at you in little javelins. A gull. A car alarm two dunes over. My own breathing, which was suddenly a *chore*, a thing with a to-do list. In. Hold. Out. Repeat until dead. Who designed this? Who looked at the elegant continuous swimming machine I used to be and thought, *no, let's make her operate a bellows manually, forever?*

The hams did not work at first.

I want to be honest about the hams. For three days they were furniture. I dragged them behind me across sand that got into places sand has no business getting, and I cursed in a language that has no swear words for *dry*, so I had to invent them, and they all sounded like coughing. I'd watch people walk past—casual, unbothered, *vertical*—balancing their entire ridiculous stack of bones on two points of contact like it was nothing, like they hadn't spent every second of their lives one bad step from a broken hip. Show-offs. Every last upright one of them.

---

And then—and I don't know how to make this land right, because it's the softest part and I keep it in my chest like a stone I found on the beach that I can't throw back—

I stood up.

Not gracefully. I stood up the way a foal does, all wrong angles and personal betrayal, gripping a railing that smelled of rust and old paint. And the hams held. My whole weight, gathered up and stacked and *carried*, and the hams just—held. Like they'd been waiting. Like they'd known something I hadn't.

There's a specific grief in learning to walk when you've spent your life in a place that carried you. The ocean never asked me to hold myself up. The ocean did it *for* me, every second, an infinite tenderness I never even noticed because I'd never known anything else. That's the trap of being held so completely—you forget you're being held. You think buoyancy is a personality trait.

Nobody carries you up here.

That was the terrible thing, and then, slowly, over weeks of falling and rust and hams, it became the beautiful thing. *Nobody carries you up here.* You do it yourself. Every step is a small argument with gravity that you somehow keep winning. You are constantly, quietly, catastrophically not-falling, and you call it walking, and you do it to the corner store, and back, humming.

I still dream in kelp. I still wake up reaching for a current that isn't there. But last week I walked to the top of a hill for no reason except that the hill was there and my hams could do it now, and I stood at the top—stood, on purpose, on two ridiculous pink miracles—and I looked out at the water that used to be me.

And I stayed on the land.

Which, it turns out, is its own way of swimming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
